prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After love discovers it, the little burn or birthmark in an odd spot he can neither see nor reach; after the internist's downturned mouth, specialists leaning over him like diviners, machines reading his billion cells; after the onslaught of insight, cures crawling through him like infestations, so many surgeries a wrong move leaves him leaking like overripe fruit; after the mountain aster and ice wine, Michigan football, CanesVenatici and the Four North Fracture Zone shrink to a room where voices grow hushed as if at some holy place, and even in the kindest eye there lurks the eternity to which he's been commended; after speech, touch, even the instinct to eat are gone, and he has become nothing but a collection of quiet tics and twitches as if something wanted out of his riddled bones, the carious maze of his brain; as the last day glaciers into his room, glass and chrome so infinites- imally facet- ed it seems he lives inside a diamond, he breaks into a wide smile, as if joy were the animal in him, blind, scrabbling, earth- covered creature tunneling up from God knows where to stand upright, feasting on distances, gazing dead into the sun.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- A hidden mark leads to a grave medical diagnosis confirmed by specialists and machines.
- The man endures invasive treatments and numerous surgeries that leave his body severely damaged.
- His once-expansive world of nature, wine, sports, and astronomy contracts to a quiet hospital room overshadowed by death.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: After, Michigan, CanesVenatici

outputs.L1: After love discovers it—the small burn or birthmark in an odd place he can neither see nor reach; after the internist’s downturned mouth, the specialists leaning over him like diviners, the machines reading his billion cells; after the onslaught of insight, cures crawling through him like infestations, so many surgeries that one wrong move leaves him leaking like overripe fruit; after the mountain aster and ice wine, Michigan football, Canes Venatici, and the Four North Fracture Zone shrink to a single room, where voices grow hushed as if in some holy place, and even in the kindest eye lurks the eternity to which he has been commended; after speech, touch, even the instinct to eat are gone, and he has become nothing but a collection of quiet tics and twitches, as if something wanted out of his riddled bones, the carious maze of his brain; as the last day glaciers into his room, the glass and chrome so infinitesimally faceted that he seems to live inside a diamond, he breaks into a wide smile, as if joy were the animal within him—a blind, scrabbling, earth-covered creature tunneling up from God knows where to stand upright, feast on distances, and gaze dead into the sun.
outputs.L2: Once love notices the small scar or birthmark hidden where he can neither look nor touch; once the internist frowns, consultants hover above him like fortune-tellers, and instruments examine every one of his billion cells; once knowledge comes crashing in and treatments swarm through his body like parasites, followed by so many operations that one careless motion makes him ooze like fruit gone soft with ripeness; once mountain asters, ice wine, Michigan football, Canes Venatici, and the Four North Fracture Zone have all contracted into a single room where people speak with the reverence of worshippers, and even the gentlest gaze contains the forever to which he has been entrusted; once he has lost language, contact, and even the urge to feed himself, becoming only a series of muted spasms and tremors, as though something were trying to escape his damaged bones and the decaying labyrinth of his mind; while the final day slowly freezes into the room, splintering glass and chrome into facets so minute that he appears to dwell within a jewel, his face suddenly opens into a broad grin—as though happiness were the creature still alive inside him, a sightless, clawing, dirt-caked animal burrowing upward from some unknowable depth, finally rising to its feet, devouring the vastness before it, and staring straight into the sun.
outputs.L3:
A hidden mark on the man’s body leads to a grave diagnosis, confirmed by specialists, scans, and the cold certainty of medical machines. What begins as a barely visible sign soon overtakes his life. He endures invasive treatments and repeated surgeries, each intended to save him but each leaving his body more damaged and exhausted.

Before his illness, his world had been expansive. He found pleasure in nature, wine, sports, and the vast mysteries of astronomy. Gradually, however, that rich landscape contracts to the confines of a quiet hospital room, where every sound and gesture is overshadowed by the approach of death. As his condition worsens, he loses the ability to speak and to respond to touch. Even his desire to eat disappears, and his life seems reduced to involuntary movements and the basic persistence of the body.

Yet on his final day, something unexpected occurs. From within the wreckage of his suffering, he smiles. It is not a faint or polite expression, but a primal, radiant joy—sudden, pure, and beyond explanation. For a brief moment, the smile seems to lift him above pain, illness, and the ruined boundaries of his body, revealing a final spark of life untouched by everything he has endured.
outputs.L4:
The passage follows a dying man from the moment of diagnosis through the long, painful course of treatment. At first, medicine offers the possibility of resistance: examinations, operations, tubes, drugs, and other invasive procedures attempt to halt the disease. Yet each intervention also marks the body more deeply. Clinical details mingle with images drawn from nature and the cosmos, making the man’s physical decline seem at once brutally intimate and part of a vast, mysterious process.

As the illness advances, the man gradually loses the ordinary powers through which he has participated in life. Speech disappears, then touch, appetite, movement, and control over his own body. The familiar self seems to recede behind damaged flesh and failing organs. His body becomes a landscape altered by disease and treatment—a place of wounds, silence, and exhaustion. The imagery continually moves between the microscopic and the immense, suggesting that what is happening inside him echoes larger cycles of decay, transformation, and renewal.

Near death, however, the passage shifts. When almost every recognizable form of expression has been taken from him, the man suddenly smiles—a wide, spontaneous smile that cannot be explained by reason or circumstance. It appears to rise from somewhere deeper than personality, language, or even conscious will. In the midst of bodily ruin, this instinctive joy survives.

The smile does not erase suffering or turn death into something simple. Instead, it reveals that life contains an irrepressible force that illness cannot entirely extinguish. At the edge of death, the man’s final expression becomes an affirmation of existence itself: mysterious, ungovernable, and radiant even in destruction.
outputs.L5: After leaving Michigan, Clara drove north beneath a clear spring sky. Far from the city lights, she stopped beside a quiet lake and searched for Canes Venatici, the small constellation known as the Hunting Dogs. Its faint stars were difficult to find, but when they finally appeared, Clara felt the distance between Earth and the heavens briefly disappear.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-sentence prose poem about a man’s progression from cancer diagnosis through invasive treatments to his final day, ending with an unexpected, radiant smile.
counterfactuals.output: From the doctor’s cold syllables through the bright knives, the poisoned drips, the tunnels of radiation, and the long nights when his body became a house dismantled room by room, he walked toward his final morning, lifted his face to the window as if someone had called his childhood name from the sun, and gave us, impossibly, a radiant smile.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, image-rich paragraph depicting terminal illness, using medical imagery, astronomical references, cherished memories, and a final moment of mysterious joy.
counterfactuals.output: The monitors blinked like a small, obedient constellation around her bed, each green pulse charting the body’s narrowing orbit, while the IV dripped its clear, medicinal rain and the oxygen tube curved beneath her nose like a fragile crescent moon. Beyond the hospital glass, evening opened its dark observatory, and she drifted through cherished galaxies: her father’s hands smelling of cedar, the summer lake holding the sky in its blue palms, her children asleep in a quilted heap after Christmas, the kitchen bright with flour and laughter. The cancer had written its black nebula through her bones, yet now pain receded to a distant star, and in the hush between one breath and the next, she lifted her eyes toward something no one else could see; astonishment softened her face, and she smiled—not farewell, not relief, but a sudden, secret joy, as if the universe had remembered her name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental literary passage about a dying patient whose world gradually contracts from travel, nature, sports, and stars to a hospital room. Use cascading “after” clauses and conclude with him smiling into death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long periodic sentence in the style of contemporary poetic prose, tracing a man’s decline from the discovery of an unseen mark through surgeries, neurological deterioration, and hospice, while avoiding sentimentality.
counterfactuals.output: After the dermatologist, parting the hair at the back of his head, found the colorless mark he had never seen and could not have seen without arranging two mirrors and turning away from himself; after the first excision widened from a neat local procedure into margins, nodes, drains, and a scar that pulled his scalp tight whenever he looked down; after the scans began naming small illuminated territories elsewhere, each one followed by a surgery whose success was measured less by what had been restored than by what had not yet been lost; after his left hand ceased to recognize coins in his pocket, his foot dragged half a beat behind him, and ordinary nouns stood at the far end of corridors he could enter but no longer cross; after the anticonvulsants thickened the hours, the steroids lifted his face into a stranger’s face, and the neurologist, tapping knee and wrist with a rubber hammer, recorded the body’s shrinking republic of responses; after he mistook the kitchen for a station, poured water into a drawer, woke speaking to someone who had died years before, and finally stopped asking why everyone watched him when he stood; after the bed was moved downstairs and then replaced by the rented bed with rails, the plastic table, the oxygen concentrator pulsing in the corner like a small indifferent engine, while the hospice nurse counted breaths, adjusted morphine by fractions, and explained that thirst could be answered with a sponge; after speech narrowed to yes, no, and once, inexplicably, the name of a childhood dog, and even those words loosened from their uses; after the house learned the schedules of gloves, syringes, linen changes, and whispered phone calls, and the unseen mark that had begun as pigmentless irregularity completed its work without revelation or lesson, he lay beneath the thin gray blanket, no longer resisting the hand that turned him toward the window, and entered the last days not as a symbol of courage or defeat but as a man whose damaged brain, failing organ by organ, had at last made the world too difficult to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the final stages of a loved one’s fatal disease through surreal metaphors—diviners, infestations, overripe fruit, glaciers, diamonds, and a buried animal—culminating in a transcendent smile.
counterfactuals.output:
In the final weeks, the diviners came without robes or wands: doctors bending over charts, nurses reading the dark tea leaves of blood. Each morning they found another omen beneath the skin.

The disease moved through you like an infestation in an abandoned house—silver mouths behind the walls, a soft industry of wings. Your body, once so certain, became overripe fruit: fragrant with memory, bruising at the gentlest touch, sweetness loosening from the stem.

Time calved around us. Great glaciers broke inside the hours and drifted away, carrying whole countries of our life together: the kitchen at dawn, your coat on its hook, the sound of your key in the door. Pain hardened in you like diamonds—clear, merciless, made by impossible pressure—while the medicines lowered their small lamps into the mine.

Sometimes, from far beneath the bed, I imagined a buried animal turning in the earth. It had slept there all your life, warm and nameless, and now it scratched once, twice, toward the surface. Then even that sound grew still.

At the end, your breath became a thread the world was too large to hold. Yet you opened your eyes. You looked beyond the diviners, beyond the ruined orchard and the melting ice, beyond every bright stone grief had made of us.

And you smiled—not as someone leaving, but as someone who had finally seen where everything goes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
